title: Don't Believe Everything You Think
alternate_titles: Don't Believe Everything You Think: Why Your Thinking Is The Beginning & End Of Suffering

editions.label: Expanded edition
editions.publisher: Authors Equity / Books By Joseph Nguyen

contents: The root cause of suffering: not events and not thoughts, but thinking
Thoughts versus thinking: spontaneous mental events versus the elaboration we add
The inside-out claim: feelings come from thought, not circumstances
Non-thinking, flow, and intuition: the mind that quiets hears its own wisdom
Goals from inspiration versus goals from desperation
Unconditional love and peace as the default state beneath thinking
Expanded-edition practice: journaling prompts, contemplative exercises, inner and outer work, and a daily journal

audiences: Overthinkers meeting thought-distancing ideas for the first time
Readers who want spiritual self-help without jargon or length
People in low-stakes distress; not a substitute for clinical care

sources.title: Don't Believe Everything You Think
sources.supports: Large-scale reader reception split between immediate help for overthinking and criticism of repetition, unsupported claims and oversimplification.
sources.limitations: Self-selected raters and edition metadata can be mixed.

sources.title: Review of Don't Believe Everything You Think
sources.supports: An adversarial therapist's critique of the thought-thinking dichotomy and missing training, alongside praise for the expanded edition's PAUSE method and presentation.
sources.limitations: Personal Substack by one therapist and philosophy PhD; an attributed adversarial view, not clinical consensus.

sources.title: Book Summary and Review: Don't Believe Everything You Think
sources.supports: A balanced clinical reading: the thought-distancing idea aligns with CBT, ACT, mindfulness and MBSR and may normalise distress; the book remains broad, repetitive, spiritual and short on structured evidence-based technique.
sources.limitations: Brief counselling-practice blog rather than peer-reviewed research.

sources.title: Don't Believe Everything You Think
sources.supports: Independent editorial characterisation of the 17-chapter book as a brief introduction to Zen, mindfulness and New Age spirituality; notes that Nguyen has no formal psychology or philosophy training.
sources.limitations: Commercial editorial review, not a clinical evaluation.

sources.title: Cognitive Defusion
sources.author_or_publisher: Miguel A. Segura-Vargas, Oxford Handbook of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy
sources.supports: Definition, exercises, measurement and empirical evidence for cognitive defusion in ACT, used to test the book's similar thought-distancing move.
sources.limitations: Does not review Nguyen's book; similarity to defusion is an editorial inference.

sources.title: Examining domains of psychological flexibility and inflexibility as treatment mechanisms in acceptance and commitment therapy
sources.supports: A systematic and meta-analytic review of 67 studies reporting that ACT interventions reduced cognitive fusion and other forms of inflexibility while increasing flexibility and defusion.
sources.limitations: Evidence concerns full ACT interventions and proposed mechanisms, not this book or its universal claims.

sources.title: The Best Books Come from the Greatest Pains: Joseph Nguyen
sources.supports: The personal origin, Zen-inspired framing, self-publishing path, reported reach and follow-up work.
sources.limitations: Friendly interview with a promotional register.
